key: He wanders on in profitless illusion: the Voice he heard yields neither fruit, nor blossom.
s: Setting those to whom Vak unveils herself against those who only hear her, the hymn turns to one called dull in friendship; Sāyaṇa, on 10.71.5, reads fruit and flower as the meaning of speech, and this man as a mere reciter without it.

evidence.words: अनन्तरमुत्तरार्धेन केवलपाठको निन्द्यते। “एषः अविज्ञातार्थः पुरुषः “अधेन्वा धेनुत्वविवर्जितया कामानामदोग्ध्र्या देवमनुष्यस्थानेषु वाक्प्रतिरूपया “मायया “चरति । किं कुर्वन् । “अफलामपुष्पाम् । वाचोऽर्थः पुष्पफलम् । अर्थवर्जिताम् ।
evidence.gloss: Then, in the second half, the mere reciter is blamed. This man, who has not understood the meaning, goes about with an illusion that is no milch cow, milking out no wishes, a semblance of speech in the places of gods and men. Doing what? Fruitless, flowerless: the meaning of speech is its flower and fruit; speech empty of meaning.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok; ref Rig Veda 10.71.5 and at [907,5] match). The plain sense places the verse after 10.71.4, which sets the one who sees and hears Vak without seeing or hearing her against the one to whom she shows herself, and before the key line of 10.71.5 comes the man called dull in friendship: faithful to Griffith’s text, and it repeats no four-word run of the key. Opened the whole Sanskrit commentary on 10.71 in the packet: at 10.71.5 Sāyaṇa says the second half blames the mere reciter (kevalapāṭhaka), glosses eṣaḥ as the man who has not understood the meaning, and says the meaning of speech is its flower and fruit, the speech he heard being empty of meaning and heard by recitation alone. The reading carries these words without drift. (Sāyaṇa takes the first half of the verse as praise of the knower, unlike Griffith’s ‘laggard’, but the sentence attributes nothing about that half to him.)
